Rose, a Republican from Tennessee, told the House Financial Services Committee that his Somaliland Economic Access and Opportunity Act , H.R. 7993, would require Treasury to report to Congress on the principal legal, regulatory and policy obstacles limiting that access. The proposed assessment would cover financial compliance standards, remittance flows, access to international financial institutions and steps that could allow Somaliland to participate in the SWIFT financial messaging system, Rose said. He said a May 2023 Supreme Court judgment dealt specifically with same-sex marriages concluded outside Namibia for immigration purposes. The Trump administration has criticised South Africa over several issues, including policies aimed at addressing racial inequality that it says discriminate against Afrikaners, descendants mainly of Dutch and French settlers. "The announcement once again, [sic] aligns with the mischaracterisation of South Africa's domestic policies by fringe groups who wrongly portray themselves as representatives of 'minorities' and Afrikaners in general," said a statement from the international relations and co-operation ministry. Announcing the restrictions on Tuesday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said: "The South African government has not adequately addressed the previously laid âout concerns." He said the visa restrictions would target those who promote "race-based discrimination, incite violence, or enable land confiscation without compensation in South Africa." stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5MgVL US President Donald Trump clashed with South African President Cyril Ramaphosa in the Oval Office in May 2025 Image: Jim Watson/AFP Advertisement The United States has announced a new visa restriction policy for South Africans amid continuing claims that the country's white Afrikaner minority is suffering from "race-based discrimination." US President Donald Trump 's administration has ⁠criticized South Africa over a range of issues including land and employment laws that are meant to redress inequalities that Black people still face 30 years after the end of apartheid . "As President Trump has made clear, the South African people are being failed by a government that is destroying its economy through an obsessive pursuit of racial grievance against the Afrikaner minority," US Secretary of State Marco Rubio claimed. "The United States will not allow such behavior to go unchecked," Rubio said. "These actions directly undermine peace, economic stability and the rule of law, and they are incompatible with the pillars of America's foreign policy." The US ambassador ‌to South ⁠Africa ⁠said ​​on ​social media ‌on Wednesday that ‌the visa restrictions were "only the first ⁠step ​in ​a ​series of ‌escalatory measures." Rubio did not name anyone who would immediately be affected but said the restrictions would target people who promote "race-based discrimination, incite violence or enable land confiscation without compensation in South Africa." South Africa: Discrimination claims based on misinformation South African President Cyril Ramaphosa says there is no evidence of discrimination against white people in his country and has called for global efforts to debunk ⁠false ​stories about white persecution. Nevertheless, the Trump administration has continued to attack South Africa. In 2025, Trump berated President Ramaphosa in the Oval Office over discredited claims of a "white genocide" in South Africa. He has also hit the country with high tariffs, boycotted a G20 summit in Johannesburg and launched a special program allowing thousands of white Afrikaners to settle in the United States. Relations between Washington and Pretoria have also nosedived over South Africa's genocide case against Israel at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) , in which it accuses the US ally of war crimes and crimes against humanity in the Gaza Strip .

stories.title: Global Gender Gap Report: Women's hard-won gains 'fragile'
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5MeN4 Women make up less than a third of lawmakers in the US Congress Image: J. Scott Applewhite/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement The Global Gender Gap Report 2026, published by the World Economic Forum (WEF) on Wednesday, reveals that gender parity worldwide is closer than ever — standing at 69.2%. However, the Geneva-based nonprofit warned that full parity may still be 120 years away and that the progress made so far remains "fragile." The report, which looked at gender parity across workforce participation, education, health and politics in 145 economies, found that women now occupy senior leadership positions in government and business at levels that were rare globally when the index began in 2006. Yet, while women's presence at the top of politics has grown since the first report, the past decade has seen that trend reverse. The percentage of countries led by women peaked in 2022 and has now fallen back to 2016 levels.

stories.title: Al-Qaida and IS-linked violence in Africa’s Sahel belt set to hit record levels this year
stories.summary: Three armed al-Shabaab fighters in Mogadishu, Somalia in 2008 – the al-Qaida-linked group is one of Africa’s deadliest. Photograph: Farah Abdi Warsameh/AP View image in fullscreen Three armed al-Shabaab fighters in Mogadishu, Somalia in 2008 – the al-Qaida-linked group is one of Africa’s deadliest. Photograph: Farah Abdi Warsameh/AP Al-Qaida and IS-linked violence in Africa’s Sahel belt set to hit record levels this year Twenty-five years after 9/11, figures compiled by conflict monitor underline how Sahel region has become centre of Islamist terror Islamist extremist violence in Africa’s Sahel region is set to reach historic highs after a series of sweeping offensives by groups linked to al-Qaida and Islamic State, according to new figures compiled by the conflict monitor Acled . As the US marks the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks launched by al-Qaida against targets in Washington and New York, the statistics underline the continued expansion of the veteran organisation in parts of Africa – in stark contrast with its relative weakness elsewhere. Compiled by Acled, which stands for Armed Conflict Location and Event Data, the statistics focus on the centre of Islamic militancy in three countries – Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger – which together comprise a huge and hotly contested zone at the heart of the strategic Sahel region.

stories.title: Slave-trade wealth was embedded in Britain’s financial system, research finds
stories.summary: The scale of the financial system’s involvement in enslavement is greater than previously known or acknowledged. Composite: Guardian/Diana Ejaita View image in fullscreen The scale of the financial system’s involvement in enslavement is greater than previously known or acknowledged. Composite: Guardian/Diana Ejaita Slave-trade wealth was embedded in Britain’s financial system, research finds Dozens of Bank of England directors and founding subscribers invested in trafficking of enslaved Africans The Bank of England and the British financial system were for centuries deeply involved in the enslavement and transatlantic trafficking of millions of African people, according to new research on Britain’s slavery history. Research by historians compiling the Register of British Slave Traders has found that the scale of the financial system’s involvement in enslavement is greater than previously known or acknowledged. The Bank of England, the central bank owned by the government since nationalisation by Clement Attlee’s Labour administration in 1946, had dozens of financiers involved in its foundation who were also significant investors in the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans.

stories.title: South Africa now probing deaths of 8 women near Johannesburg
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5MduC South African police have warned women to exercise caution amid fears the cases could be connected Image: AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement South African police are now investigating the deaths of eight women found east of Johannesburg over the past two months, after another body was discovered on Tuesday and an earlier case was added to the widening investigation. The deaths have raised fears that a serial killer or group of killers could be operating in the area. Several of the victims were found naked or partially clothed, with some showing signs of sexual violence. "The challenge is ahead of us and the deaths of these young women must not be in vain," acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia told reporters following a meeting to discuss the killings. What have South African police said? The South African Police Service (SAPS) has issued a public warning urging women to exercise caution when jogging or carrying out similar activities in the area. "While investigations are still underway and SAPS has not, at this stage, confirmed that the deaths are linked to a serial killer, the similarities are sufficiently concerning for the police to issue a public warning and intensify investigations," police spokesperson Athlenda Mathe said.

stories.title: More than 1,000 women invested in companies at heart of Britain’s slave trade
stories.summary: Several 18th-century paintings depict affluent white women with young enslaved servants, who often wore a single pearl earring. Composite: Guardian/Palesa Monareng View image in fullscreen Several 18th-century paintings depict affluent white women with young enslaved servants, who often wore a single pearl earring. Composite: Guardian/Palesa Monareng More than 1,000 women invested in companies at heart of Britain’s slave trade Women used profits from trafficking of enslaved Africans to secure their families’ futures, research reveals More than 1,000 women invested in the slave trade, challenging the conventional notion that they were passive beneficiaries and largely fought for its abolition. Researchers found women bought, sold and brokered shares in the Royal African Company, South Sea Company, and other separate ventures, and used profits from the trafficking of enslaved Africans to secure financial independence and provide for their families. By the time the RAC, which trafficked about 150,000 enslaved people, was dissolved in 1752, women made up about 10% of shareholders.

stories.title: The London hospital funded by donors who invested in the slave trade
stories.summary: Illustrations by Diana Ejaita The London hospital funded by donors who invested in the slave trade Barts is one of many UK institutions whose benefactors were involved in the trafficking of enslaved Africans Inside the Great Hall of St Bartholomew’s North Wing, alongside stately portraits of the apostle from whom London’s oldest hospital takes its name and King Henry VIII, extravagant commemorative boards adorn the walls. The Great Hall was a grand, formal space where governors weighed their philanthropic donations and drafted their wills, many while investing in the stock of companies built on the trafficking of enslaved Africans. Today, many of those donors are commemorated in acrylic gold paint on the boards. The Register of British Slave Traders , a joint venture between Lancaster University, the University of Manchester and University College London, includes biographical data on every known investor in Britain’s transatlantic trafficking of enslaved African people from the 16th to 19th centuries. It reveals how wealthy individuals , often enriched by the proceeds from racialised chattel enslavement, donated to hundreds of church parishes and helped to fund schools, hospitals and charities across the country.

stories.title: Africa's richest man Dangote's IPO out of reach in Nigeria
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5Ma1u "Of the people, by the people, for the people" — or rather a market-driven strategy_ Image: Sodiq Adelakun/REUTERS Advertisement The industrialist Aliko Dangote is turning to Nigerians to help finance the next growth phase of his oil refinery : The richest man in Africa announced that he is seeking to attract about $1.6 billion (€1.4 billion) by going public. This initial public offering of Dangote Industries is intended to help support a $14.3 billion expansion, which would more than double the refinery's production capacity. In absolute numbers, it would increase capacity from 700,000 barrels per day (bpd) to 1.4 million bpd. It would also include new petrochemical and refining units designed to reduce Nigeria 's reliance on imports of some petrochemical products while also allowing the plant to produce different grades of diesel. This plan would make the refinery one of the largest single-site refining complexes in the world.

stories.title: How Britain's kings and queens powered the slave trade – video
stories.summary: How Britain's kings and queens powered the slave trade – video How Britain's kings and queens powered the slave trade – video Enslaved African people were seared with hot metal brands bearing the royal crown, according to research by historians who have documented the monarchy’s centuries-long involvement in Britain’s slave trade. The kings and queens most heavily involved were those who ruled after the monarchy was restored in 1660. The Register of British Slave Traders is the most comprehensive research project into the investors in the country's trafficking of enslaved African people. Its publication will further inform calls for the king to finally acknowledge the monarchy’s deep involvement in the trade. In response to the Guardian’s reporting of the new research relating to the monarchy, a spokesperson for King Charles said he was 'grateful to all those undertaking academic work in this area and thus contributing to the debate about how such issues might best be addressed'.

stories.summary: A composite of archival material relating to Britain’s involvement in transatlantic slavery. From left: Sir John Hawkins, English naval commander and administrator and slave trader, his face overlaid with a ledger recording enslavers and cotton suppliers and their links to English investors; an account of sums awarded by the Commissioners of Slave Compensation, Parliamentary Papers 1837-38; and a photograph of enslaved African Americans in a cotton field in South Carolina, 1863-66. © Senate House Library Composite: Guardian/Diana Ejaita/© Senate House Library View image in fullscreen A composite of archival material relating to Britain’s involvement in transatlantic slavery. From left: Sir John Hawkins, English naval commander and administrator and slave trader, his face overlaid with a ledger recording enslavers and cotton suppliers and their links to English investors; an account of sums awarded by the Commissioners of Slave Compensation, Parliamentary Papers 1837-38; and a photograph of enslaved African Americans in a cotton field in South Carolina, 1863-66. © Senate House Library Composite: Guardian/Diana Ejaita/© Senate House Library Explainer What is the Register of British Slave Traders and whom does it identify? Three years of research has uncovered 13,000 people who invested in Britain’s trafficking of enslaved Africans The Register of British Slave Traders is the product of three years of research by a team of historians into all known investors in Britain’s near 250 years of trafficking enslaved African people, from the 16th to 19th centuries. It provides profiles and biographical details of thousands of people who financed the British slave trade, which violently trafficked approximately 3 million African men, women and children across the Atlantic.

stories.title: A spoonful of sugar: how South Africa’s weigh-and-pay shops are tackling ‘poverty tax’ head on
stories.summary: One of the shops runs by Gcwalisa – which means ‘fill up’ in isiZulu – in Johannesburg’s Alexandra township. Photograph: Julie Bourdin View image in fullscreen One of the shops runs by Gcwalisa – which means ‘fill up’ in isiZulu – in Johannesburg’s Alexandra township. Photograph: Julie Bourdin A spoonful of sugar: how South Africa’s weigh-and-pay shops are tackling ‘poverty tax’ head on Run by a social enterprise, the six shops operate from shipping containers across Johannesburg’s Alexandra township and sell food and household goods by weight in small, affordable amounts Every morning, on her way to the laundry shop she runs in Johannesburg’s Alexandra township, Tsholofelo Mphela stops at a bright yellow shipping container to buy a few spoonfuls of sugar. Inside, shelves are lined with large jars of beans, rice and maize meal, and clear boxes filled with breakfast cereal and loose teabags. A tap dispenses cooking oil by the millilitre.

stories.title: The royal crown branded on enslaved Africans: Britain’s monarchy and the slave trade
stories.summary: A close-up of a King Charles’s eyes beneath a jewelled crown, with silhouetted figures and ships collaged above Composite: Guardian/Diana Ejaita View image in fullscreen A close-up of a King Charles’s eyes beneath a jewelled crown, with silhouetted figures and ships collaged above Composite: Guardian/Diana Ejaita The royal crown branded on enslaved Africans: Britain’s monarchy and the slave trade From Elizabeth I’s backing of early voyages to royal investment in trafficking companies, generations of monarchs were central to Britain’s slave trade Enslaved African people were seared with hot metal brands bearing the royal crown, according to research by historians who have documented the monarchy’s centuries-long involvement in Britain’s slave trade. The Register of British Slave Traders identifies thousands of people who invested in Britain’s trafficking of enslaved Africans, including kings and queens. In response to the Guardian’s reporting of the new research relating to the monarchy, a spokesperson for King Charles said he was “grateful to all those undertaking academic work in this area and thus contributing to the debate about how such issues might best be addressed”. Dr Nicholas Radburn, a historian at Lancaster University, discovered evidence of the branding in the archives of the South Sea Company, a British crown-backed enterprise that trafficked thousands of enslaved African people to plantations in the 1700s. Radburn found a letter sent by the company’s board to its agents in Buenos Aires, instructing them to brand enslaved people with hot metal.

stories.title: Monarchs, MPs and merchants: the register laying bare Britain’s slave-trading past
stories.summary: The register builds the most comprehensive single picture so far of those who perpetrated the enslavement of African people. Illustration: Diana Ejaita/The Guardian View image in fullscreen The register builds the most comprehensive single picture so far of those who perpetrated the enslavement of African people. Illustration: Diana Ejaita/The Guardian Monarchs, MPs and merchants: the register laying bare Britain’s slave-trading past Exclusive: New research identifies thousands who profited from trafficking enslaved Africans and traces some financial links to institutions still operating today The big picture The Register of British Slave Traders and the president of Ghana, John Dramani Mahama The enormous scale of Britain’s centuries-long trafficking of enslaved African people, supported by parliament and the monarchy, has been laid bare by new research. The Register of British Slave Traders , the product of a three-year project by a team of specialist historians, documents the investors in Britain’s near 250-year transatlantic slave trade from the first traffickers in the 1560s to abolition in 1807. The register provides biographical detail for as many of 10,500 investors as possible from historical records, building the most comprehensive single picture so far of those who perpetrated the enslavement of African people.

stories.title: ‘Spraying should be the last option’: how farmers are exploring alternatives to pesticides
stories.summary: Pesticide use in Kenya has risen steadily over the last few decades, with imports more than doubling between 2015-19 Photograph: Imago/Alamy View image in fullscreen Pesticide use in Kenya has risen steadily over the last few decades, with imports more than doubling between 2015-19 Photograph: Imago/Alamy ‘Spraying should be the last option’: how farmers are exploring alternatives to pesticides When pesticide proved no match for the insect, desperate Phyllis Nvuda tried a new way to save her infested orchard F or two decades, Phyllis Nduva, 72, has grown mangoes and citrus in Wote, a town in Kenya’s eastern Makueni County. In the beginning, she only had to worry about ordinary fruit flies. She handled them simply, buying chemical pesticides and spraying her trees whenever they appeared. But then, in 2014, the false codling moth turned up on her farm. The small brown creature had been causing havoc in South Africa for years, and in 2007 it was spotted in Kenya.

Oyo made global headlines in 1995 when he took the throne at the age of three.

stories.title: 'It's like a dog set loose on us' - fear over Kenya's crackdown on foreign traders
stories.summary: Image source, BBC/Brian Khisa Image caption, Burundian tuk-tuk driver Ndaikech Ali says Kenya, which has been so welcoming to him for years, now feels hostile By Basillioh Rukanga Published 12 September 2026 For Ndaikech Ali, who has been traversing the streets of the Kenyan capital eking out a living as a tuk-tuk driver for the past nine years, Nairobi's traffic - not xenophobia - has been his biggest concern. During his time in the East African nation, the Burundian says he has always found Kenyans to be friendly and welcoming - that is until last week, when the president ordered a crackdown on foreigners working as traders or operating small-scale businesses. "Now they have turned against us," he told the BBC at the Burundian embassy in Nairobi where many have been queuing this week for documents to allow them to travel back home. "The threats are manyâ¦ even from children," he said, adding: "It's a like a dog has been set loose upon us. We have been bitten." President William Ruto made his remarks last week when addressing Kenyan traders gathered at state house - in reference to legislation before parliament that seeks to exclude foreign nationals from petty trade and to mandate the local sourcing of certain materials. During his speech, he said that all foreign nationals operating small businesses had until 7 September to pack up shop, saying such low-level jobs should be reserved for Kenyans. Ali, like others, panicked, saying it seemed the president's announcement had been interpreted by some Kenyans as a signal that foreign nationals were no longer welcome in the country. "We face harassment and can't work," he says. "If our work is stopped, we lose the income that enables us to pay rent and buy food.

stories.title: Uber leaves 2 key African markets — and drivers in despair
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5MRuX Uber has become part of daily life for people across the world, like here in Australia. But financial shortcomings have forced the ride-hailing app to shrink its footprint in Africa Image: Xinhua/picture alliance Advertisement A week ago, Uber unexpectedly announced its departure from the Nigerian market after spending more than a decade building up its presence in Africa's most populous country. The ride-hailing platform also said it would be winding up its operations in Uganda — also with immediate effect. With the exit from both Nigeria and Uganda , Uber now remains operational only in a handful of African countries — Egypt, Ghana, Kenya, and South Africa. "This decision is limited strictly to these two markets and does not impact our operations across the rest of the continent," Uber said in a statement, adding that their "immediate priority is supporting drivers, riders, and local team members throughout this transition," without sharing details on what this assistance would entail. In the last year, the multinational company also closed shop in Ivory Coast and Tanzania, while also cutting its global workforce by 10%.
